notes_list.title: E2 Stereochemistry and Anti-Periplanar Geometry
notes_list.basic_overview: E2 elimination is stereospecific when conformationally defined because C–H and C–X bonds are removed in a concerted step. Anti-periplanar alignment is normally favored.
notes_list.extra_info_content: The reacting C–H and C–X bonds align anti-periplanar, allowing optimal orbital overlap and simultaneous bond breaking/forming. In cyclohexanes, trans-diaxial geometry is required for the classical E2 pathway.
notes_list.examples: 2-bromobutane gives different alkene ratios depending on conformation and base. Cyclohexyl bromides often require axial leaving group and axial β-H.
notes_list.conditions_and_medium: Strong base; solvent, base size and substrate substitution affect competition with SN2 and product distribution.
notes_list.mechanism_steps: 1. Identify β-carbons. 2. Find β-H. 3. Determine anti-periplanar conformer. 4. Draw concerted electron flow. 5. Predict alkene geometry and regioselectivity.
notes_list.kinetics_and_energy: One kinetic event breaks C–H and C–X while forming π bond. Rate depends on substrate and base concentrations for bimolecular E2.
notes_list.selectivity_and_stereochemistry: Links kinetics, conformation, stereochemistry and regioselectivity.
notes_list.common_traps: Do not predict E2 from connectivity alone when conformational restriction matters.

exam_focus.level: IIT-JAM / MSc entrance / GATE concept depth
